stack.heading: Accelerating access to affordable, sustainable, safe and resilient digital infrastructure for children

items.body: Digital markets were never designed to serve children. 2.2 billion people remain offline, not by choice, but because the economics of last-mile connectivity were never built to reach them. 1.3 billion children have no internet at home, more than 500 million students have no internet access at all, and in Africa families pay around five times the global average for mobile data.

The cost falls on children. A learner without a connection can’t reach digital classrooms; an offline clinic can’t track immunisations or flag at-risk cases in time; an unregistered child stays invisible to the systems meant to protect them. As the services children depend on shift onto digital rails, those same children risk being left out of the AI revolution before it ever reaches them. Where the infrastructure is weak, systems fail quietly, at scale.

The reverse is also true. A connected clinic can track every child’s immunisations and flag those at risk in time; a connected school can reach digital and AI-powered learning; a connected registration point makes a child visible to the systems meant to protect them.

items.label: UNICEF’s Digital Inclusion
items.body: team works to ensure that no child is left behind in the digital world. Together with governments, technology partners, development finance institutions and the private sector, we help expand access to affordable, sustainable, safe and resilient digital infrastructure.

We take a proven model (map, procure, finance) and apply it across the systems children depend on: schools, health facilities, emergencies, and social and child protection. One live platform gives governments, partners and investors a shared, real-time picture at facility level.

The pattern is consistent across every country case. Where facilities are mapped and costed, governments plan with greater confidence and implementation moves faster. Where procurement is organised, markets respond with better pricing and service quality. Where monitoring is routine, attention shifts from access alone to performance and reliability. Because governments contract, monitor and own the result, connectivity becomes national infrastructure, embedded in policy, budgets and delivery.

A model that already works, country after country. Through Giga, the UNICEF and ITU initiative to connect every school to the internet, we have spent the past several years proving this approach in education, and the results speak for themselves.

UNICEF Digital Inclusion supports governments to connect public child-facing facilities through technical assistance, digital tools, data analysis, financing support, and guidance on procurement and service delivery, so that they have the connectivity they need to serve children, families and communities better.

items.label: Mapping
items.body: Connecting facilities starts with knowing where they are and which remain offline. We bring data sources together, map child-facing facilities on Giga Maps and advise on the data needed to assess connectivity.

items.label: Procurement
items.body: We advise on market assessment, competitive bidding, contract design and service-level monitoring, helping governments cut costs, improve quality and manage provider performance.

items.label: Financing
items.body: We build investment cases and identify financing: public budgets, donor funding, loans, Universal Service Funds, private partnerships, blended finance and mechanisms such as Connectivity Credits.

stack.heading: UNICEF Digital Inclusion and Estonia, 2023-2026 and beyond

items.body: Estonia has been a valued and far-sighted partner to UNICEF, through Giga. Its early support, a two-year grant of €120,000 channelled through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 2023-2024, helped deliver concrete results in Kenya and Namibia and laid the groundwork for Giga’s procurement work.

When the partnership began, Giga was a pilot initiative supporting 19 countries and 5,700 connected schools, backed by a handful of seed funders. Today, it provides active support across 54 countries, with a focus on Central Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and Central America, and a further 25 countries, including Ukraine, have expressed interest. Giga has mapped 2.3 million schools and connected and supported more than 140,000 of them, helping over 42 million young people access a safe and empowering internet.

items.label: Namibia.
items.body: By the end of 2024, we had mapped 1,900 schools in Namibia and infrastructure analysis was still underway. Building on that foundation, infrastructure modelling has been completed, giving the Government an evidence base to plan connectivity investments. 1,300 schools are now connected, with 671 still to go, as the Government works toward its goal of connecting 80% of all schools by 2030. To track connectivity quality and target investment, Namibia’s Ministry of Education, Arts and Culture now uses Giga Meter, a real-time monitoring app developed at the Giga Technology Centre in Barcelona.

items.label: Kenya.
items.body: Estonia’s contribution helped catalyse collaboration between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of ICT. That collaboration produced a roadmap to connect 1,000 schools, backed by €9.8 million in EU funding. At the time, procurement was still being finalised and connectivity costs were high. Today, Kenya shows how competitive procurement can cut the cost of school connectivity. Giga supported the development of a multi-vendor model, which helped reduce average monthly connectivity costs by around 60%, from US$110-120 to about US$45 per school. More than 600 schools have been connected through this model. Kenya is also one of four pilot locations for Giga’s Connectivity Credits, which reward internet service providers with tradeable digital credits for connecting schools, helping to make connectivity financially sustainable.

items.label: Market shaping.
items.body: In 2024, Giga’s procurement work focused on analysing the barriers to affordable connectivity, with plans to scale procurement strategies across countries. Today, Giga has operationalised its Global Procurement Facility in Geneva, in collaboration with UNICEF Supply Division. This delivers the ambition Giga outlined to Estonia in 2024: moving beyond fragmented, country-by-country tenders to a pooled, transparent and competitive model.

Giga has framed a US$6 billion opportunity to connect over 520,000 schools and 260,000 health centres across Africa and, working with Smart Africa and the UN Economic Commission for Africa, secured expressions of interest from 16 African countries to pursue connectivity through coordinated, pooled approaches. Building on this, Giga launched a continent-wide tender through the Global Procurement Facility to support African governments in procuring connectivity services. Over 100 suppliers are preparing their bids, and the tender will establish Long-Term Agreements: pre-negotiated contracts that governments can buy from through UNICEF, giving them price benchmarks and lowering costs.

stack.heading: Shaping the next phase together: opportunities for renewed partnership

items.label: Universal basic compute
items.body: Connectivity is only half of AI access: schools and other child-facing public institutions also need affordable computing power. UNICEF Digital Inclusion is exploring a model of universal basic compute (UBC), under which every connected school would receive a baseline allocation of compute credits for child-safe AI tools, hosted on shared regional infrastructure, purchased in bulk through the Global Procurement Facility and monitored through Giga Meter. Estonia could help turn this into practice by co-designing the governance and data-protection model, piloting UBC in connected schools in a chosen country, and funding a feasibility study to build the evidence base for EU and Team Europe co-financing.

items.label: Connectivity for AI readiness
items.body: Children cannot benefit from AI without meaningful connectivity: enough bandwidth, low latency and reliable quality, verified in real time through Giga Meter. We have already supported the Government of Uzbekistan in assessing school connectivity for AI readiness. Building on that work, Estonia could co-develop a joint connectivity benchmark for AI-ready schools, drawing on lessons from AI Leap, and help extend Giga Meter with new layers that measure AI readiness.

items.label: Transparent procurement on a shared platform
items.body: Giga’s Global Procurement Facility, run with UNICEF Supply Division, replaces fragmented country-by-country tenders with pooled, competitive procurement. The next step is a digital procurement platform where contracts are open, prices are comparable and service delivery is checked against real connectivity data. Estonia could help build it by contributing its expertise in e-procurement and interoperability to the platform’s design, and supporting its rollout in partner countries such as Kenya and Namibia.

stack.heading: Accelerating access to affordable, sustainable, safe and resilient digital infrastructure for children

items.label: UNICEF’s Digital Inclusion
items.body: team advises, advocates and acts so that children are neither excluded from nor left behind in the digital world. Together with governments, technology partners, development finance institutions and the private sector, we work to accelerate access to affordable, sustainable, safe and resilient digital infrastructure for every child. This strengthens the public services children rely on across education, health, protection and emergency response, while creating opportunity in the digital economy.

The Digital Inclusion team works with governments to tailor integrated packages of open-source solutions, technical assistance and advisory services to their digital transformation ambitions, resources, ecosystem readiness and timing. Our package combines in-country support in 190 countries and territories, with mapping and real-time monitoring, finance and sustainable business models, market shaping and procurement, ecosystem development, and evidence. Together, these capabilities enable governments to plan, build, own, manage and sustain digital infrastructure at scale, delivering reliable and equitable digital public services for children. They also strengthen markets for technology providers, from multinational companies to local small and medium-sized enterprises.
Digital markets were not designed to reach every child. Last-mile costs, fragmented demand and weak procurement leave essential services without reliable infrastructure.

usPartnerships.footerLabel: Digital Inclusion Partnerships with U.S. Based Companies

stack.heading: Digital Inclusion Partnerships with U.S. Based Companies

items.body: UNICEF's Digital Inclusion works to accelerate affordable, sustainable, safe, and resilient digital infrastructure, including the connectivity, compute, and AI-enabling infrastructure children need, so that no child is excluded from or left behind in the digital world, and every child can safely and equitably access the public services and economic opportunity it unlocks.

U.S. companies are central to that model, supplying infrastructure capacity, technical expertise, and capital that make connectivity viable at scale. Below: where those partnerships stand today, and the specific, live asks in front of U.S. companies, carriers, hyperscalers, and the FCC to build the next wave.

items.label: Active U.S. Patnerships
items.body:
# Equinix
Equinix Foundation partners with UNICEF, investing specifically in Connectivity Credits, an innovative model that incentivizes internet service providers to connect and sustain school connectivity through discounted backhaul access, making it more affordable for ISPs to deliver reliable connectivity to schools over the long term. Equinix also contributes technical expertise and access to its global infrastructure to help identify connectivity gaps, deliver access to remote and underserved schools, and improve online learning experiences for students worldwide.
- Provided digital infrastructure capacity at its São Paulo data center, dedicated high-capacity connectivity, managed security, and technical onboarding support, powering a proof of concept of the connectivity measurement platform, which collects more accurate data on real internet quality. UNICEF aims to replicate the model in other regions, including Africa.
- Over the past six months, Equinix technical expertise has helped frame how to expand Connectivity Credits toward fiber capacity, IP transit, and data center integration. Equinix is already funding the first wave of pilots; this sets the stage for a second wave linked to Equinix infrastructure. The Equinix Nigeria team and Giga are refining a small-scale pilot and follow-on proposal.
# Cloudflare
Cloudflare partnered with UNICEF to bring real-time data from Cloudflare's Speed Test into Giga Maps, helping better measure and monitor internet connectivity at schools around the globe, a critical step in helping governments and nonprofits advocate for and implement better connectivity solutions where they're needed most.
- Runs up to 10 million availability tests per month directly from schools, collecting data on speed, latency, and affordability to power Giga Maps, giving governments, the private sector, and civil society the data they need to plan investments and track progress.
- Cloudflare's global network, data centers in over 330 cities worldwide, is positioned to minimize latency and deliver accurate, real-time connectivity assessments globally.
# Internet Society
There is no standard way of measuring the internet, it's complex, highly technical, and yet affects everyone. UNICEF Giga is working with Internet Society to combine technical expertise, research, and community-building to better understand how connectivity is measured, where the gaps are, and how to close them. The collaboration launched at Pulse Research Week at Giga's Technology Center in Barcelona, convening measurement experts to explore meaningful connectivity, identifying needs, testing solutions, and validating frameworks. The two organizations continue to jointly develop more transparent, reliable, and inclusive approaches to measuring the internet.
# Mapbox
Provides the geospatial and mapping infrastructure behind Giga's school-connectivity data, powering the maps and location analysis used to measure the real-world impact of school connectivity.
# Maxar
Maxar's satellite imagery helps Giga identify and geolocate schools worldwide, supporting the effort to connect millions of young people to the internet by pinpointing where connectivity is needed most.

items.label: Open asks and needs, Not yet partners
items.body:
# Satellite / LEO Backhaul
- **Starlink (SpaceX)**: A formalized “impact backhaul” wholesale pricing agreement, discounted satellite capacity for ISPs that keep a verified school or health facility connected, checked daily through Connectivity Credits. A detailed proposal is already in front of them; no agreement yet.
- **Amazon Leo**: Early engagement now, so its capacity becomes a second LEO source alongside Starlink in the same marketplace once commercially available.
- **Skylo Technologies**: A third candidate worth engaging in parallel, already has a live commercial direct-to-device deal with T-Mobile, a useful near-term proof point for the same backhaul model.
# Terrestrial Backbone, Tier 1 IP Transit & Data Center
- **Cogent, AT&T, Lumen, GTT Communications, Zayo**: “Impact pricing” on IP transit, passed through the chain so Tier 2 carriers can offer better pricing to the Tier 3 ISPs that actually connect schools.
- **Digital Realty, Vantage Data Centers, CyrusOne**: Impact-priced data center space and interconnection, the same model as the existing Equinix partnership, extended to additional U.S. data center operators.
# Hyperscalers & African Subsea Capacity
AI is driving the largest subsea build cycle in two decades, led by **Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft**.
- Introductions to hyperscalers and cable consortium members already investing in African subsea capacity, for wholesale capacity, IRU, or landing-partnership arrangements. Meta's 2Africa cable, one of the largest, just completed its core buildout, a live, current hook for this conversation.
- **SubCom**, the U.S. subsea cable manufacturer and installer that physically builds many hyperscaler-backed systems, is also a concrete introduction target, it sits underneath most of these projects and just closed a $2.3B raise for AI-driven subsea demand.
- Work with the FCC on how an open-access, trusted-vendor wholesale layer in Africa fits broader U.S. priorities on secure, resilient, diversified international connectivity infrastructure.
# Spectrum Certificates, Regulatory Standards
- U.S./FCC sandbox: Integrate the Spectrum Certificates registry with current spectrum management tools; prove the framework's value for responsiveness and telecom resilience; build management-platform tools; work with FCC innovation partners on granular spectrum sharing. Federated Wireless, an FCC-approved CBRS Spectrum Access System administrator already running a live registry, is a natural technical integration partner.
- International traction: Strong regulatory interest from Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana, plus an early-stage pilot in Sierra Leone. Seeking further FCC introductions and support as deployments continue.
- Emerging technologies: Unmanned-vehicle communication, LEO satellite communication, and dynamic spectrum sharing for emergency response. Seeking partnerships with technology providers, including Starlink, Amazon Leo, and Skylo (above), with FCC backing.
- Partnership development with space tech developers and operators, and with standards bodies such as the IESG and ISE.
# Financial institutions, Founders
- Connect with U.S. development finance institutions and other U.S.-backed instruments for pre-seed/seed investment, guarantees, or blended finance.
